## How Questions Reach The Ballot

A question has a history before we see it on a ballot. The measures in our guides include City Council–referred proposals and citizen petitions. Those are different routes to a public vote—not endorsements or a promise that a particular office will carry out the result.

The [Baltimore City Board of Elections](https://www.baltimorecity.gov/boe/ballot-question-text) links City questions to Council records and identifies the voter-petition route. Some questions ask permission to borrow for specified purposes; others propose changes to the City Charter. Our guides identify the type and origin so we can see what kind of decision is being put to us.

## Why We Keep Watching {#a-result-isnt-the-whole-story}

A result tells us what voters approved or rejected. It does not, by itself, show that a project is finished, bonds have been issued, or money has been spent. The distinction between authorization and follow-through matters.

These are the questions we want to keep in view:

- Who is responsible for the next decision?
- What deadlines, ordinances, budgets, or other steps does the measure call for?
- What records would show what actually happened?
- Where is there a specific opportunity for residents to ask questions or take part?

The guides are the foundation for that work, not a claim that every implementation step has already been investigated. We do not have to agree on how we voted to care about what follows.
